content.content:
\TYP{BottomType} is the bottom of the type hierarchy:
all types are supertypes of \TYP{BottomType}.
For types $T$ and $U$,
we write $T \Ovrsubtype U$ when $T$ is a subtype of $U$,
and $T \strictsubtype U$ when $T \Ovrsubtype U$ and $T \neq U$;
in the latter case,
we say $T$ is a \emph{strict} subtype of $U$.
We also say that $T$ is a \emph{supertype} of $U$ if $U$ is a subtype of $T$.
Thus, in the execution of a
valid Fortress program, an expression's runtime type is always a subtype of
its static type.
We say that a value is \emph{an instance of} its runtime
type and of every supertype of its runtime type; immediate subtypes of
\TYP{Any} comprises of tuple types, arrow types, \TYP{()}, and \TYP{Object}.

The exclusion relation is a symmetric relation between two types
whose intersection is \TYP{BottomType}.
Because \TYP{BottomType} is uninhabited
(i.e., no value has type \TYP{BottomType}),
types that exclude each other are disjoint:
no value can have a type that is a subtype of two types that exclude each other.
\note{
The converse is technically not true: we can define two traits with
 method declarations
 such that no trait or object can extend them both, so no value can have a
 type that is
 a subtype of both trait types, but the trait types do not exclude each
 other.  For example:
 trait A f(self, y: Object) = 1; end
 trait B f(x: Object, self) = 2; end
 trait C f() = 3; end

No pair of the three trait types defined above can be extended
but none of them exclude any of the others.
}
Note that \TYP{BottomType} excludes every type including itself
(because the intersection of \TYP{BottomType} and any type is \TYP{BottomType}),
and also that no type other than \TYP{BottomType} excludes \TYP{Any}
(because the intersection of any type $T$ and \TYP{Any} is $T$).
\TYP{BottomType} is the only type that excludes itself.
Also note that if two types exclude each other
then any subtypes of these types also exclude each other.


Fortress also allows \emph{coercion} between types
(see \chapref{conversions-coercions}).  A coercion from $T$ to $U$
is defined in the declaration of $U$.  We write $T \coercedefto U$ if
$U$ defines a coercion from $T$.  We say that $T$ \emph{can be coerced
to} $U$, and write $T \coercesto U$, if $U$ defines a coercion from
$T$ or any supertype of $T$: $T \coercesto U \iff \exists T':
T \Ovrsubtype T' \logicand T' \coercedefto U$.


The Fortress type hierarchy is acyclic with respect to both subtyping and
coercion relations except for the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item The trait \TYP{Any} is a single root of the type hierarchy and it
forms a cycle as described in \chapref{lib:object}.
\item There exists a bidirectional coercion between two tuple types if and
  only if they have the same sorted form.
\end{itemize}

These relations are defined more precisely
in the following sections describing each kind of type in more detail.
Specifically,
the relations are the smallest ones that satisfy
all the properties given in those sections (and this one).


\section{Trait Types}
\seclabel{trait-types}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{Type} &::=& \emph{TraitType} \\
\end{Grammar}

A \emph{trait type} is a named type defined by a trait or object declaration.
It is an \emph{object trait type}
if it is defined by an object declaration.
\note{
Victor: The following text really belongs to traits, not to types.
Traits are declared by trait and object declarations
(described in \chapref{traits} and \chapref{objects}).
A trait has a \emph{trait type} of the same name.}

A trait type is a subtype of every type
that appears in the \KWD{extends} clause of its definition.
In addition, every trait type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.

A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
in which case the defined trait type
excludes every type that appears in that clause.
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.

Two instantiations of the same parameterized trait exclude each other
unless each static argument of one,
other than an operator argument,
is the same as the corresponding static argument of the other:
the same type for a type parameter,
and the same value for a \KWD{nat}, \KWD{int}, \KWD{bool},
dimension, or unit parameter.
This property is called \emph{instantiation exclusion}.
Operator arguments do not count:
an operator argument names the operator that a subtrait inherits
(\secref{opr-ident}),
so instantiations that differ only in their operator arguments,
such as the instantiations of \TYP{BooleanAlgebra}
that \TYP{Boolean} extends (\secref{lib:boolean}),
do not exclude each other on that account.
Because types that exclude each other are disjoint,
no type is a subtype of two instantiations of one parameterized trait
that differ in a static argument other than an operator argument;
the rule that this imposes on trait and object declarations
is stated in \secref{trait-decls}.
\revision{revival-rule}{The Working Draft of February 2011 stated no
exclusion between instantiations, so the relations defined in this chapter,
the smallest ones that satisfy the properties given,
let a type be a subtype of two different instantiations of one
parameterized trait.
The paragraph above adds the property.

(* A tuple type whose element types are all Index types is an Index and no Object, so a static parameter bounded by Index takes ZZ32 and its pairs and triples, and the subscript beside the range subscript runs at each. *)
component TupleIndexBoundWalk
export Executable

ident[\I extends Index\](x: I): I = x

trait Cells[\I extends Index\]
    opr[i: I]: String
    opr[r: Range[\I\]]: String
end

object Grid[\I extends Index\]() extends Cells[\I\]
    opr[i: I]: String = "one index"
    opr[r: Range[\I\]]: String = "a range"
end

object Slot(n: ZZ32) extends Index end

kind(x: Object): String = "object"
kind(x: Any): String = "any"

run(): () = do
    assert(ident(3), 3, "ident takes a ZZ32 at its bound Index")
    assert(ident((1, 2)), (1, 2), "ident takes a pair of ZZ32 at its bound Index")
    assert(ident((1, 2, 3)), (1, 2, 3), "ident takes a triple of ZZ32 at its bound Index")

    g1 = Grid[\ZZ32\]()
    assert(g1[4], "one index", "the subscript at ZZ32")
    assert(g1[0#2], "a range", "the range subscript at ZZ32")
    g2 = Grid[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]()

(* A tuple type whose element types are all Index types is an Index and no Object, so a static parameter bounded by Index takes ZZ32 and its pairs and triples, and the subscript beside the range subscript runs at each. *)
component TupleIndexBoundWalk
export Executable

ident[\I extends Index\](x: I): I = x

trait Cells[\I extends Index\]
    opr[i: I]: String
    opr[r: Range[\I\]]: String
end

object Grid[\I extends Index\]() extends Cells[\I\]
    opr[i: I]: String = "one index"
    opr[r: Range[\I\]]: String = "a range"
end

object Slot(n: ZZ32) extends Index end

kind(x: Object): String = "object"
kind(x: Any): String = "any"

run(): () = do
    assert(ident(3), 3, "ident takes a ZZ32 at its bound Index")
    assert(ident((1, 2)), (1, 2), "ident takes a pair of ZZ32 at its bound Index")
    assert(ident((1, 2, 3)), (1, 2, 3), "ident takes a triple of ZZ32 at its bound Index")

    g1 = Grid[\ZZ32\]()
    assert(g1[4], "one index", "the subscript at ZZ32")
    assert(g1[0#2], "a range", "the range subscript at ZZ32")
    g2 = Grid[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]()
    assert(g2[1, 2], "one index", "the subscript at a pair")
    g3 = Grid[\(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]()
    assert(g3[1, 2, 3], "one index", "the subscript at a triple")

    m: Matrix[\RR64,2,2\] = matrix[\RR64,2,2\](2.0)
    m[0,1] := -3.0
    assert((m + 1.0)[0,1], -2.0, "a matrix plus a number")
    assert((1.0 + m)[0,0], 3.0, "a number plus a matrix")
    assert((m MAX 0.0)[0,1], 0.0, "a matrix MAX a number")
    assert((0.0 MAX m)[0,0], 2.0, "a number MAX a matrix")

    a = array[\ZZ32\](2,3).fill(0)
    a[1,2] := 12
    assert(a[1,2], 12, "a rank-2 array read and written at a[i, j]")
    assert(a[(1,2)], 12, "a rank-2 array read at a pair")

    assert(instanceOf[\Index\](3), true, "a ZZ32 is an Index")
    assert(instanceOf[\Index\]((1, 2)), true, "a pair of ZZ32 is an Index")
    assert(instanceOf[\Index\]((1, 2, 3)), true, "a triple of ZZ32 is an Index")
    assert(instanceOf[\Index\]((1, "a")), false, "a pair with a String element is no Index")
    assert(instanceOf[\Index\]("a"), false, "a String is no Index")
    assert(instanceOf[\Object\](3), true, "a ZZ32 is an Object")
    assert(instanceOf[\Object\]((1, 2)), false, "a pair of ZZ32 is no Object")
    assert(kind(3), "object", "a ZZ32 goes to the declaration over Object")
    assert(kind((1, 2)), "any", "a pair of ZZ32 goes to the declaration over Any")

    s = Slot(5)
    assert(instanceOf[\Index\](s), true, "an object of the program's own that extends Index is an Index")
    assert(instanceOf[\Object\](s), true, "an object of the program's own that extends Index is an Object")
    assert(instanceOf[\Index\]((s, 1)), true, "a pair of such an object and a ZZ32 is an Index")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

(** Assertion *)
assert(flag:Boolean): () =
    if NOT flag then
        fail("Assertion failed!")
    end

assert(flag: Boolean, failMsg: String): () =
    if NOT flag then
        fail(failMsg)
    end

assert(x:Any, y:Any, failMsg: Any...): () =
    if x =/= y then
        xs = typecase x of
                 x':Object => x'.asDebugString
                 else => "" x
             end
        ys = typecase y of
                 y':Object => y'.asDebugString
                 else => "" y
             end
        msg = xs " =/= " ys "; " (BIG || failMsg)  (* use || here instead of loose juxt *)
        fail(msg)
    end

(*)true : Boolean = () SEQV ()
(*)false : Boolean = true SEQV ()

(** Uniform random distribution within the given `range`. It uses a classic

object UniformDistribution[\T\](range:FullRange[\T\])

(** Uniform random distribution within the given `range`. It uses a classic
    retrial method. **)
object UniformDistribution[\T\](range:FullRange[\T\])
    extends RandomDistribution[\T\]

    min[\N extends Integral[\N\]\](gen:RandomGen[\N\]): Just[\T\] = Just[\T\](range.forward().left.get)
    max[\N extends Integral[\N\]\](gen:RandomGen[\N\]): Just[\T\] = Just[\T\](range.forward().right.get)

    (* XXX the current implementation requires the range of N is greater than
       the range of T *)
    generate[\N extends Integral[\N\]\](gen:RandomGen[\N\]): T = do
        spacing = (gen.max.get - gen.min.get + 1) DIV |range|
        retrybound = gen.min.get + |range| spacing
        x: N := gen.random()

(described in \chapref{traits} and \chapref{objects}).
A trait has a \emph{trait type} of the same name.}

A trait type is a subtype of every type
that appears in the \KWD{extends} clause of its definition.
In addition, every trait type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.

A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
in which case the defined trait type
excludes every type that appears in that clause.
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.

\subsection{Object Trait Types}
\seclabel{object-traits}

...
A tuple type consists of a parenthesized, comma-separated list
of two or more types.

Every tuple type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.
No other type encompasses all tuple types.
Tuple types cannot be extended by trait types.

content.content:
\subsection{The type of \KWD{self} in a trait with a self-type parameter}
\seclabel{revival-self-type}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{idn-ref}; \secref{trait-decls}; \secref{methods}.
\item[Change] In \secref{idn-ref}, a sentence after the one on the self-type
idiom: in a declaration of a trait \VAR{T} with no \KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists only ``\EXP{\ldots}'', and a
self-type parameter \VAR{X}, \KWD{self} has the type \EXP{T \cap X} in the bodies of
the trait's methods, and the \KWD{self} parameter keeps the type \VAR{T} in the
signature of each method declaration.
In \secref{trait-decls}, a paragraph after the one on \KWD{comprises} clauses
defines a self-type parameter: a static parameter of a trait with no
\KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists only ``\EXP{\ldots}'', that is bounded by the trait at its own static
parameters, or by an instantiation of a trait with a self-type parameter that the
trait also lists in its \KWD{extends} clause, with that static parameter as the
static argument for the self-type parameter.
The paragraph requires every trait or object declaration and every object
expression that extends an instantiation of such a trait to be a subtype of
the static argument of that instantiation for the self-type parameter, a trait
standing as the type of \KWD{self} in its bodies, the intersection of its type with the types
its \KWD{comprises} clause lists or with its own self-type parameter, and gives an example marked ``Not allowed''.
In \secref{methods}, a box after the sentence that a functional method's
\KWD{self} parameter implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object
says that the sentence still holds of the declaration's signature.
Each of the three passages has a box.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
revival's decision of 13~October 2026 on the bodies of the self-typed traits,
and its second form of a self-type parameter, through a trait that the trait
extends, follows a default taken under that decision on 14~October 2026.
\library\ declare their orders and their algebra as traits whose static
parameter is bounded by the trait itself, as in
\EXP{\KWD{trait}\;\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I \KWD{extends} \TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket\rrbracket},
and give them default bodies that return \KWD{self} where that parameter is
declared, or pass it where the parameter is expected: the team's minimal
complete definitions, such as \OPR{MIN} on \TYP{StandardTotalOrder} and
\VAR{floor} on \TYP{Integral}.
The interpreter runs them; the compiled type checker refused 29 of them,
since it typed \KWD{self} as the trait.
A bound constrains the static argument, not \KWD{self}: an object may extend
\EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket} without being a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a body that treats \KWD{self} as the parameter is sound
only if every declaration that extends the trait is a subtype of its static
argument for that parameter.
Scala states that rule for its declared self types (``The self type of a class
or object must conform to the self types of all classes which are inherited by
the template'', \emph{Scala Language Specification 2.13}, section 5.1); the revival reads the self type from the bound, which \library\
already write, as the team's compiled type checker reads it from a
\KWD{comprises} clause (\secref{idn-ref}), a reading that the team's gated test
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXX10k.test} pins.
Naden's account of the Return Type Rule (2012) asked that the self-type idiom
become ``a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but
instead only in bounds''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex}, lines 626--630).
The signatures keep the type of the trait because the type group's account of
overloading of 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019) assumes, for the
completeness of its matching of types, that no declared type holds a type
parameter inside an intersection (pp.~11:21--22), and its Return Type Rule
compares declared domains (p.~11:13): with the intersection in the signatures,
the domains of the two declarations of \OPR{CMP} on \TYP{StandardPartialOrder}
and \TYP{StandardTotalOrder} became equivalent, and the compiled type checker
reported 18 errors of the Return Type Rule that the declarations do not make.
The second form of a self-type parameter keeps valid as written the mixins of
\library\ that the team wrote in 2009, \TYP{ContainmentBySubset} and
\TYP{ContainmentByComparison}, whose static parameter is bounded by the trait
\TYP{Containment}, which they extend at it.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/self-typed-bodies-judgement.md} and
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-self-type/decision-record.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker types \KWD{self} as \EXP{T \cap X} in
the bodies of the dotted and functional methods of a trait with a self
parameter \VAR{X}, keeps \VAR{T} in the signatures that overloading, the Return
Type Rule and the choice of a declaration at a call read, and refuses a trait
or object declaration or an object expression that the new paragraph of
\secref{trait-decls} does not allow, with the message
``\VAR{D} extends \EXP{C\llbracket{}A\rrbracket}, whose self parameter is \VAR{A},
but \VAR{D} is not a subtype of \VAR{A}.''.
The interpreter has no static types: it runs the bodies as before, and loads a
declaration that the paragraph refuses.
The code generator compiles a default body that returns \KWD{self} as the self
parameter with no conversion to the type of the instance, so a program that
runs such a body, which the compiled type checker now accepts, with the parameter at an object type
fails the JVM's verification when the body's class is loaded (row~695 of the revival's gap
ledger).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex},
lines 53--54 and 64--69, which stand unchanged and are now followed by the new
sentence:
\begin{quote}
The type of \KWD{self} is the type of the trait or object being declared by
the innermost enclosing trait or object declaration or object expression.
\end{quote}
and
\begin{quote}
If the innermost enclosing such construct is a trait declaration (for a trait
called, say, `\EXP{T}'), and that trait declaration has a \KWD{comprises}
clause, and `\EXP{U_1}', `\EXP{U_2}', ..., `\EXP{U_n}' are the traits mentioned
in the \KWD{comprises} clause, then the type of \KWD{self} is instead
``\EXP{T \cap (U_{\mathrm{1}} \cup U_{\mathrm{2}} \cup \ldots \cup U_{\mathrm{n}})}''.
\end{quote}
The paragraph of \secref{trait-decls} is new.
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, line 486, the end of the
sentence of \secref{methods} that the new box follows, stands unchanged:
\begin{quote}
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] Under route~C a self-typed trait is read by a \KWD{comprises}
clause that lists its static parameter, as the compiled path's own library
declares its orders (\nolinkurl{Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi}, lines 16 and 24,
in the revival's repository); under such a clause the self-type idiom of
\secref{idn-ref} types \KWD{self}, and this rule is not reached.
A return to that form would need the clause on the self-typed traits of
\library, which would also close each of them to its static parameter; a way
for the interpreter past its stack overflow on a clause that lists a static
parameter (row~407 of the revival's gap ledger); and leave in
\secref{trait-decls} for a static parameter as a listed type, which the type
group's calculus of 2012 does not admit.
\end{description}

This specification is a working draft;
it is meant to include all language features included in
the Fortress Language Specification, Version 1.0\EXP{\beta{}}
(perhaps with additional ) and any language changes since then.
This version of the specification is not yet for a release;
it may include wild ideas that require additional research before they can be
implemented reliably.
This specification includes descriptions of unimplemented features in boxes
at the beginning of sections,
and informal comments and notes in boxes in the margin.\\


In 2026 the Fortress revival revised this working draft where a decision
taken for the implementation it is completing would otherwise leave the
text and the implementation in disagreement.
The first such revision states the type group's rule that no type is a
subtype of two different instantiations of one parameterized trait, which
the compiled type checker enforces for type arguments and numerals, with the exceptions \appref{spec-changes} names, and this draft had
not stated, and
rewrites the examples that the rule refuses.
Each revised passage carries a box headed ``Revised by the 2026 revival'';
\appref{spec-changes} lists every change with its reason, the original
text, and the alternative not taken.
\end{figure}

\item generic overloading check

\item keyword and varargs parameters
\item varargs expressions
\item some modifiers (\KWD{override}, \KWD{io}, \KWD{atomic}, \KWD{value}, ...)
\item qualified names

#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage with the full overloading check: the gate's distance/run.sh, with the
# shadowed OverloadingChecker (checker-shadow.py beside this script) compiled by scalac and
# put ahead of everything on the run's class path.
#
#     explorations/perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/run-shadow.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> [export] [catch]
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with the call set up as the fortress-repo skill says, after
# ant compileAll. With `export`, the export check's isDeclaredName admits symbolic names too;
# with `catch`, a checker crash on one name is printed and the check goes on (checker-shadow.py).
# The scratch directory gets the shadow source and classes, the copy of run.sh (whose one
# changed line puts $EXTRA_CP first on the java class path), and the run's own scratch
# (run.txt, errors.tsv) under <scratch-dir>/d.
set -u
OUT=${1:?usage: run-shadow.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> [export]}
SC=${2:?usage: run-shadow.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> [export]}
case "$SC" in /*) ;; *) SC="$PWD/$SC" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
P="$FH/explorations/perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2"
mkdir -p "$SC/ocsrc" "$SC/occlasses" || exit 1
rm -f "$SC"/ocsrc/*.scala
rm -rf "$SC/occlasses"/* 
python3 "$P/checker-shadow.py" "$FH" "$SC/ocsrc" "${@:3}" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" | tail -1)
java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -nowarn -classpath "$CP" -d "$SC/occlasses" -encoding UTF-8 \
     "$SC"/ocsrc/*.scala || { echo "run-shadow: scalac failed" >&2 ; exit 1 ; }
sed 's#-cp "\$SCRATCH/shadow-classes:#-cp "${EXTRA_CP:+$EXTRA_CP:}$SCRATCH/shadow-classes:#' \
    "$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh" > "$SC/run.sh"
grep -q 'EXTRA_CP' "$SC/run.sh" || { echo "run-shadow: run.sh's class path line moved" >&2 ; exit 1 ; }
# run.sh finds its helpers through $FORTRESS_HOME, so the copy may live anywhere
EXTRA_CP="$SC/occlasses" bash "$SC/run.sh" "$OUT" "$SC/d"

87	## 10. Decisions, findings, questions
88	
89	**Decisions.**
90	
91	1. I shared only answers whose computation read no context. This chooses exactness over reach. The alternatives:
92	   - TypeScript's rule, dualized: a true answer found under the history's cuts is true without them. It shares
93	     more, but it can change nested answers, and with them the per-analyzer normal forms.
94	   - Keys renamed apart, plus the variables' bounds, shared across analyzers.
95	   - Fuel or depth limits, which change answers.
96	   - Library-side changes: drop `IntLiteral` from `Number`'s clause, or keep `T extends Number`. These change the
97	     library, not the checker.
98	2. Only `True` and `False` are shared, not constraint formulas.
99	3. A hit in the analyzer's own memo counts as a context read. This is conservative.
100	4. The memo lives on `TraitTable`, behind its own switch, following rung M.
101	5. The refusal test carries the `XXX` prefix, by the team's convention.
102	
103	No decision of the curator covers 1 to 5.
104	
105	**Findings for the record.**
106	
107	- The slowdown is recomputation, with the numbers of §2 and §3.
108	- The count stage on this tree takes about 300 s for the base, measured once at load 0.31. That is not "seconds",
109	  and the base's `checkApi FortressLibrary` takes 74 s under the fix.
110	- The overloading stage's error order is not fixed between runs (by reading, §7).
111	- Noticed by reading, not verified: `withClauseParams` decides by name whether a type variable in an excludes
112	  clause is in scope (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:820`). So an analyzer whose own parameter has the same name as the
113	  clause's could read the clause through its own bound. The fix counts that test as a context read.
114	
115	**Questions for the curator (decisions not taken).**
116	
117	- Q1: carry the fix as a rung ahead of fork 2's library half, or with it, or hold both until the distance stage's
118	  remaining gap (1,032 s against 819 s at the landed gate, not a pair) is also closed?
119	- Q2: pursue the further exact steps of §9?
120	
121	**Commands worked out.**
122	
123	- **Compile the fix into a shadow folder.** Two Scala files at once:
124	  `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d <dir> -encoding UTF-8 TraitTable.scala TypeAnalyzer.scala`.
125	  Then prefix `<dir>` to the classpath in copies of the stage scripts.
126	- **Run compiled `.test` files through the harness on shadow classes:**
127	  `FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "<dir>:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit <absolute .test paths>`.
128	- **JFR with deep stacks:**
129	  `-XX:FlightRecorderOptions:stackdepth=2048 -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=...,settings=profile,dumponexit=true`.
130	  `jcmd <JVM pid> JFR.dump name=1 filename=...` takes a copy mid-run, and
131	  `jfr print --events jdk.ExecutionSample --stack-depth 2048` reads it.
132	  - The default 250 MB cap keeps only the last few minutes.
133	  - Aim `jstack` and `jcmd` at the `java` process, never at the stage's `timeout` wrapper. A dump aimed at the
134	    wrapper killed a run.

content.content:
\seclabel{subscripting-ops}

A subscripting operator method declaration has
\KWD{opr} where a method declaration would have an identifier.
The value parameter list, rather than being surrounded by parentheses,
is surrounded by a pair of brackets.  A subscripting operator method
declaration may have any number of value parameters, keyword parameters,
and varargs  parameters in that
value parameter list.  Static parameters may also be present, between
\KWD{opr} and the left bracket.  Any paired
Unicode brackets may be so defined \emph{except} ordinary
parentheses and white square brackets; in particular, the square
brackets ordinarily used for indexing may be used.

An expression consisting of a subexpression immediately
followed (with no intervening whitespace) by zero or more
comma-separated expressions surrounded by brackets will
invoke a subscripting operator method declaration.  Methods
for the expression preceding the bracketed expression list are
considered.  The compiler considers all subscripting operator method
declarations that are both accessible and applicable, and the most
specific method declaration is chosen according to the usual overloading
rules.  For example, the expression \EXP{\VAR{foo}_p} might invoke the
following subscripting method declaration because expressions in the square
brackets are rendered as subscripts:
\input{\home/advanced/examples/OprDecl.Subscripting.tex}

p='Specification/appendices/changes.tex'
s=open(p).read()
anchor='\\subsection{Passages not yet revised}\n'
assert s.count(anchor)==1
entry=r'''\subsection{The index type of a subscript}
\seclabel{revival-index}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{type-relations}; \secref{trait-types};
\secref{tuple-types}; \secref{trait-decls}; and, in a draft build, the item on
array indexing among the proposed features of the appendix ``Internal
Document''.
\item[Change] \library\ declare the trait \TYP{Index},
\EXP{\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{Index} \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Any}}, which
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} extends and \TYP{Range} excludes, and bound every index
parameter of their generic indexed types by it,
\EXP{I \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Index}}: \TYP{Indexed}, its delegated and mutable
forms, the array traits, the full ranges, and the mapped, reversed and
index-value views over an indexed generator.
\TYP{BoundedRange}, whose index type stays unbounded since the open range
\EXP{(:)} is a range over \TYP{Any}, keeps its narrowed \VAR{atMost}, whose
result is a full range, under the method condition
\EXP{\KWD{where} \{ I \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Index} \}}.
In \secref{tuple-types}, a sentence says that a tuple type whose element types
are all subtypes of \TYP{Index} is a subtype of \TYP{Index}, and no subtype of
\TYP{Object}; the sentence on the exclusion of non-tuple types names
\TYP{Index} beside \TYP{Any}, and says that a tuple type excludes \TYP{Index}
if and only if one of its element types excludes \TYP{Index}.
In \secref{trait-types}, the sentence that every trait type excludes every
tuple type excepts \TYP{Index}.
In \secref{type-relations}, the immediate subtypes of \TYP{Any} include
\TYP{Index}.
In \secref{trait-decls}, the sentence on the implicit extension of
\TYP{Object} names \TYP{Index} beside \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object}, a sentence
says that a trait that extends \TYP{Index} and no other trait but \TYP{Any}
implicitly extends \TYP{Object} too, and the hierarchy is rooted at
\TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index}.
The item on array indexing among the proposed features gains a box, and so
does each changed passage.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
revival's decision of 23~October 2026 on the index type of \library's
subscripts, and its place of \TYP{Index} outside \TYP{Object} and its
\VAR{atMost} follow the revival's answers of the same day.
The bound finishes the team's wish.
Their item on array indexing calls \TYP{Indexed}'s two subscripts, one over an
index and one over a range of indices, ``not really a valid overloading'', and
goes on: ``We want to say that the type variable \VAR{I} extends a type, say,
\TYP{Index} which either excludes \EXP{\TYP{Range}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket} or is
a supertype of \EXP{\TYP{Range}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex}, lines 200--203).
With \VAR{I} bounded by an \TYP{Index} that \TYP{Range} excludes, the two
subscripts never apply to one value, and the pair is a valid overloading at
every instance (\secref{overloading-static-params}); unbounded, at the instance
\TYP{Any} the range subscript is the more specific, and its result is no
element, which the Return Type Rule refuses.
The compiled type checker, made to check the overloading of symbolic operators
over \library, reported 124 such errors in the generic indexed types, and none
at the bound with the rule below.
The tuple rule is the revival's departure from the designers' text on tuple
types.
The team named the obstacle themselves: ``However, we cannot say that because
when we invoke that subscripting method, we write \EXP{a[1, 2, 3]} where the
arguments are passed as a tuple, \EXP{(1, 2, 3)}. If we want to use
\TYP{Index}, we need a magic to convert that tuple argument expression to
something of type \TYP{Index}.'' (lines 204--207).
They asked for a conversion, and a conversion would change every index value
that a subscript passes; the rule makes the tuple type a subtype of
\TYP{Index} instead, a typing rule that changes no value.
The Working Draft forbids it three times (quoted below), and the team's later
Types chapter twice: ``Every trait type excludes \TYP{()}, \TYP{BottomType} and
every tuple type.'' and ``A tuple type excludes \TYP{BottomType}, \TYP{()}, and
every trait type, arrow type or function type.'' (Luchangco, 2012,
\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines 341
and 424, in the revival's repository).
\TYP{Index} stands outside \TYP{Object}, as \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object} do, so
that a tuple of indices is no \TYP{Object} (\secref{revival-bound}); the
specification's library declares its trait of all tuples so too,
\EXP{\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{Tuple} \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Any}
\KWD{excludes} \{\,\TYP{Object}\,\}} (\secref{core-tuple}).
Two ways stay open, each with its own cost: a constraint
\EXP{\KWD{where} \{ I \KWD{excludes}\:\TYP{Range}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket \}},
which the team left as an open question (the item ``Type variables in
\KWD{excludes} clauses'' of the same appendix) and which is not among the
Working Draft's forms of constraint; and subscripts by a range only at the
index types that \library\ fix, as the arrays of rank one to three, the strings
and \TYP{Maybe} already have them, at the price of slicing in the generic
views.
A reversal would remove the rule, the bound and \TYP{Index}, and leave the 124
errors standing, or take one of the two ways.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-index-bound/decision-record.md} in
the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The interpreter and the compiled type checker, when it checks
\library, read the rule and the exclusion by the qualified name of
\library's trait, so a program's own trait named \TYP{Index} is not read as
it, and both keep \TYP{Index} outside \TYP{Object}; a program with an index
type of its own declares it an \TYP{Index}.
A program's own generic declaration that instantiates an indexed type of
\library\ at its own type parameter bounds that parameter by \TYP{Index}; the
compiled type checker refuses it unbounded, ``The static argument \VAR{I} does
not satisfy the corresponding bound \TYP{Index}'', and the interpreter, which
checks a bound only at a call that infers the parameter, runs it.
The compiled path still compiles programs against its own library, which
declares no \TYP{Index}, until it is switched over to the interpreter's.
The code generator refuses a method with a \KWD{where} clause of its own
(row~701 of the revival's gap ledger), so after the switch-over
\TYP{BoundedRange}'s \VAR{atMost} waits on that row, beside the two
\VAR{distribute} methods of \library's sum reduction.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex},
lines 134--136, 215--216, 263--265 and 272--273:
\begin{quote}
We say that a value is \emph{an instance of} its runtime type and of every
supertype of its runtime type; immediate subtypes of \TYP{Any} comprises of
tuple types, arrow types, \TYP{()}, and \TYP{Object}.
\end{quote}
\begin{quote}
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type, and the
special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.
\end{quote}
\begin{quote}
Every tuple type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}. No other type encompasses all tuple
types. Tuple types cannot be extended by trait types.
\end{quote}
\begin{quote}
A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type other than \TYP{Any}.
\end{quote}
which stand unchanged but for the first, second and fourth, and
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, lines 181--183 and
193--194:
\begin{quote}
In addition, every trait except \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object} implicitly extends
the trait \TYP{Object} if it does not do so explicitly.
\end{quote}
\begin{quote}
This relation must form an acyclic hierarchy rooted at trait \TYP{Object}.
\end{quote}
The box in the appendix of proposed features is new.
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

'''
s=s.replace(anchor, entry+anchor)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
grep -n 'revival-index' Specification -r | head

### 3.3 The covariance example, E1 (`basic/trait-parameters.tex`)

Original:

Base `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-351`; the Working Draft of February 2011, `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-351` (the same text, compared by `git hash-object`):

```latex
Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of
themselves. For example, we can write:
%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
In this declaration, for every subtype \VAR{S} of \VAR{T}, \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket}
is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}. Effectively, we have expressed
  the fact that the static parameter \VAR{S} of \VAR{C} is covariant.
```

New text: `trait-parameters.tex:351-397`. The declaration kept, with "(* Not allowed! *)" added as the first line of its `%` source and of its typeset block, the typeset lines otherwise byte for byte; the sentence that it would express covariance and is not allowed; "Static parameters are invariant: C[\S\] is a subtype of C[\T\] only if S and T are the same type"; the widening function:

```
trait C[\S\]
  getter item(): S
end
object CItem[\S\](item: S) extends C[\S\] end
widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\] = CItem[\T\](c.item)
```

and the callout, whose `covariant` sentence is: "The type group's later design declares variance instead with a covariant modifier on a static parameter (the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012), which is implemented on neither the interpreter nor the compiled path; the revival's decision record and row 404 of its gap ledger say what is known of it."

Reason: judgement section 3.1, E1, option 1; the library's widening functions (`Library/CovariantCollection.fss:15-36`, `upward[\R, I extends R, T extends R\]` and `opr APPCOV[\T, A extends T, B extends T\]`). The widening example as printed, completed into a program with a `Dog` and an `Animal`, prints `dog` under `walk` and compiled (`probes/examples/SpecWiden.fss`, `.walk.txt`, `.compile.txt`, `.run.txt`); the judgement's `AltCovariantBounded`, with `Any` bounds, does the same (`explorations/reviews/spec-refused-examples/captures/AltCovariantBounded.walk.txt`, `.run.txt`).

The `covariant` keyword, the type group's later direction. The later chapter's prose: "A static parameter of a trait declaration may be declared with the covariant modifier. In this case, it is a covariant parameter of the generic type defined by the trait declaration. One instantiation of a generic type is a subtype of another instantiation of the same generic type if the argument instantiating each covariant parameter in the first instantiation is a subtype of the corresponding argument in the second instantiation, and the argument instantiating each non-covariant parameter is the same in both instantiations." (`types.tick:322-339`, its comment lines left out); and its exclusion between instantiations: "Two instantiations of a generic trait type exclude each other if the corresponding arguments for any covariant parameter exclude each other, or if the corresponding arguments for any non-covariant parameter are not type equivalent." (`types.tick:357-360`). The keyword entered the grammar in `26718e298` (2011-12-06) and subtyping by variance in `20a8febe9` (2012-02-29) (ledger row 404). Today the compiled checker accepts it and the compiled run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`, while `walk` refuses the binding (`explorations/reviews/spec-refused-examples/captures/AltCovariantVariance.compile.txt`, `.run.txt`, `.walk.txt`; row 404). It is the road by which declaration-site variance can return, once both paths carry it to run time (worklist item 12, `POSITIONS.md:131`); the text mentions it in one callout sentence and specifies nothing of it, since it runs on neither path.

Route C: the same under route C (section 3.2).

#!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../explorations/experiment/env.sh"

LADDER_ROOT="${LADDER_ROOT:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/ladder-r1}"
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"
export LADDER_TMP="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-tmp"
export FORTRESS_CACHES="$LADDER_CACHES"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx2g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=$LADDER_CACHES -Djava.io.tmpdir=$LADDER_TMP"

PRISTINE="$LADDER_ROOT/pristine"

mkdir -p "$RAW/tests" "$RAW/not_working_library_tests" "$LADDER_TMP"

disk_guard () {
    local free
    free=$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}')
    if [ "$free" -lt "$MIN_FREE_KB" ]; then
        echo "STOP: only ${free} KB free on / (floor ${MIN_FREE_KB} KB)" | tee -a "$OUT/ladder.log"
        exit 2
    fi
    echo "-- disk free ${free} KB, cache $(du -sm "$LADDER_CACHES" | cut -f1) MB"
}

# Step 1: the compiler-world library, in the order repo-internals.md gives.
build_library () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    local f
    for f in LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss ; do
        echo "library: $f"
        timeout 600 ../bin/fortress compile "$f" || { echo "LIBRARY BUILD FAILED on $f"; exit 1; }
    done
}

# Step 2: one known-good compiled program must print PASS before the ladder starts.
sanity () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    timeout 200 ../bin/fortress compile library_tests/Integer1.fss > /dev/null 2>&1 || return 1
    timeout 60 ../bin/fortress run Integer1 2>&1 | grep -q PASS
}

# Keep only the library's own cache entries; a program's entries are never reused.
prune_cache () {
    ( cd "$LADDER_CACHES" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.now"
    ( cd "$PRISTINE" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.keep"
    comm -23 "$LADDER_TMP/.now" "$LADDER_TMP/.keep" | while read -r p; do
        rm -f "$LADDER_CACHES/$p"
    done
}

component_of () {
    # component/api name as declared, which is what `fortress run` wants
    sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*\(component\|api\)[[:space:]]\+\([A-Za-z0-9_.]\+\).*/\2/p' "$1" | head -1
}

run_one () {
    local corpus="$1" path="$2"
    local base name comp crc rrc t0 t1 ct rt
    base=$(basename "$path")
    name="${base%.*}"
    comp=$(component_of "$path")
    [ -n "$comp" ] || comp="$name"

    t0=$(date +%s)
    timeout -k 5 "$COMPILE_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress compile "$path" \
        > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.compile" 2>&1
    crc=$?
    t1=$(date +%s); ct=$((t1-t0))

    rrc=""
    rt=""
    if [ "$crc" -eq 0 ] && [ "${base##*.}" = "fss" ]; then
        t0=$(date +%s)
        timeout -k 5 "$RUN_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress run "$comp" \
            > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.run" 2>&1
        rrc=$?
        t1=$(date +%s); rt=$((t1-t0))
    fi

    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
        "$corpus" "$base" "$comp" "$crc" "$rrc" "$ct" "$rt" >> "$TSV"
    echo "$corpus/$base crc=$crc rrc=$rrc ${ct}s"
}

main () {
    echo "=== ladder start $(date -Is) ==="
    disk_guard
    if [ ! -d "$PRISTINE" ]; then
        build_library
        rm -rf "$PRISTINE"; cp -a "$LADDER_CACHES" "$PRISTINE"
    fi
    sanity || { echo "SANITY FAILED: library_tests/Integer1 did not print PASS"; exit 1; }
    echo "sanity ok: library_tests/Integer1 compiles and prints PASS"
    prune_cache

    : > "$TSV"
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1

    local n=0 line corpus f
    while IFS=$'\t' read -r corpus f; do
        [ -n "$corpus" ] || continue
        run_one "$corpus" "$corpus/$f"
        n=$((n+1))
        rm -rf "${LADDER_TMP:?}"/fortress*rats
        if [ $((n % 10)) -eq 0 ]; then prune_cache; disk_guard; fi
    done < "$OUT/subset.txt"
    prune_cache
    echo "=== ladder done $(date -Is), $n files ==="
    disk_guard
}

<!-- The decision record of climb batch 21's rung B: the specification's passages that the index bound and the tuple rule revise (P-156), each with its original, its new text, its reason and the way back. -->
# Decision record: the index type of a subscript

The decision is P-156 (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`), with the answers to climb batch 21's questions 1 and 2 (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-21.md`, section 2), and fork 9 of that record, which the type-decisions judgement asked for (`explorations/reviews/type-decisions-review/judgement.md`, V2 and section 2, item 1). The Appendix I entry is `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, "The index type of a subscript", `\seclabel{revival-index}`. Every box below cites it.

## 1. The rule and the bound, in short

- The library declares `trait Index extends Any end` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1245`, `.fss:1947`). `ZZ32` extends it, `Range` excludes it, and every index parameter of the library's generic indexed types is bounded `I extends Index`.
- A tuple type whose element types are all subtypes of `Index` is a subtype of `Index`. A tuple type excludes `Index` if and only if one of its element types excludes `Index`.
- `Index` extends only `Any`, as `Object` does, so a tuple of indices is no `Object`. A type that extends only `Index` (and `Any`) extends `Object` too.

## 2. Why the bound: the team's wish

The Working Draft's appendix of proposed features, item "Array indexing" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:200-207`):

> The above overloaded declarations are not really a valid overloading. We want to say that the type variable I extends a type, say, Index which either excludes Range[I] or is a supertype of Range[I]. However, we cannot say that because when we invoke that subscripting method, we write a[1, 2, 3] where the arguments are passed as a tuple, (1, 2, 3). If we want to use Index, we need a magic to convert that tuple argument expression to something of type Index.

The bound is the first branch of their wish. Unbounded, `opr[i: I]` beside `opr[r: Range[\I\]]` is invalid at `I = Any`: the range subscript is the more specific there, and its result `Indexed[\E,I\]` is no `E` (row 783). The compiled checker, made to read symbolic operators, reported 124 errors of this family over the library (F-245).

## 3. Why the rule is the revival's departure

The team asked for a conversion. A conversion would change each index value that a subscript passes (`explorations/perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md`, section 3.1). The rule makes a tuple type a subtype of a trait type instead, which the designers' tuple-type text forbids:

- Working Draft, `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:215-216`: "Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type, and the special types () and BottomType."
- Working Draft, `:272-273`: "A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type other than Any."
- The 2012 Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:341`: "Every trait type excludes \Void, \Bottom\ and every tuple type."; `:424`: "A tuple type excludes \Bottom, \Void, and every trait type, arrow type or function type."

The judgement (V2) keeps the rule as the least costly way and asks that it be recorded as a departure. The ways kept open: S5, a constraint `where { I excludes Range[\I\] }` (the team's open question, `future.tex`, item "Type variables in excludes clauses"); W3, range subscripts only at the fixed index types.

## 4. The passages

### 4.1 The immediate subtypes of `Any` (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex`, "Relationships between Types")

Original (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:134-136`, the same in the base `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:151-153`): "...immediate subtypes of Any comprises of tuple types, arrow types, (), and Object."

New (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:151-159`): "...immediate subtypes of Any comprises of tuple types, arrow types, (), Object, and Index, the trait of the types that a subscript takes, of which a tuple type whose element types are all subtypes of Index is a subtype", with a box.

Reason: `Index extends Any` makes it an immediate subtype of `Any`. Way back: drop the clause and the box.

### 4.2 Trait types and tuple types (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex`, "Trait Types")

Original (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:215-216`; base `:232-233`): quoted in section 3.

New (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:238-246`): "Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and the special types () and BottomType, and every trait type other than Index excludes every tuple type; Index excludes a tuple type only where one of its element types excludes Index", with a box.

Reason: the exclusion is the dual of the rule; without it the text says that `Index` excludes the tuple types that are its subtypes, the contradiction that the probe's checker patch left (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:560` at the base). Way back: the original sentence.

### 4.3 The rule (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex`, "Tuple Types")

Original (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:263-269`): "Every tuple type is a subtype of Any. No other type encompasses all tuple types. Tuple types cannot be extended by trait types. Tuple types are covariant: ..." These stand unchanged.

New (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:335-340`), after the covariance sentence: "A tuple type whose element types are all subtypes of the trait Index is a subtype of Index, the trait of the types that a subscript takes. Index extends Any and not Object, so such a tuple type is no subtype of Object."

Reason: section 3. Way back: remove the two sentences.

### 4.4 The exclusion of non-tuple types (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex`, "Tuple Types")

Original (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:272-273`; base `:323-324`): quoted in section 3.

New (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:342-351`): "A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type other than Any and Index, and it excludes Index if and only if one of its element types excludes Index.", with a box for 4.3 and 4.4.

Reason: as 4.2. Way back: the original sentence.

### 4.5 The implicit extension of `Object` (`basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations")

Original (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex:181-183`; base `Specification/basic/traits.tex:186-188`): "In addition, every trait except Any and Object implicitly extends the trait Object if it does not do so explicitly." and (`:193-194`; base `:198-199`) "This relation must form an acyclic hierarchy rooted at trait Object."

New (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:186-195`, `:205-210`): `Index` named beside `Any` and `Object`; two sentences say that `Index` extends only `Any`, as `Object` does, and that a trait that extends `Index` and no other trait but `Any` implicitly extends `Object` too; the hierarchy "rooted at the traits Object and Index"; a box.

Reason: question 1's answer, option 1 (P-156): a tuple of indices is an `Index` and never an `Object`, as P-42 keeps tuples out of `Object`. The second sentence keeps the rule that every other trait is an `Object` true of a type that a program declares an `Index` (fork 8): without it, `object Slot(n: ZZ32) extends Index end` would be no `Object` (the desugarer adds `Object` only to a clause that names nothing but `Any`). Way back: the original sentences, and `Index` declared as an ordinary trait, which question 1's options 2 and 3 describe.

### 4.6 The proposed feature (`appendices/future.tex`, "Traits and Objects", item "Array indexing")

Original (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:200-207`), quoted in section 2, stands unchanged.

New (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:208-214`): a box "Done, by subtyping in place of a conversion", naming `Index`, `ZZ32`, `Range`'s exclusion, the bound and the rule.

Way back: remove the box.

## 5. BoundedRange's `atMost`

Question 2's answer, option 2 (P-156): `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\] where { I extends Index }` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2258`, `.fss:4106`), the library's form for a member that applies at some instances only (`SumReduction`'s `distribute`s, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3438`, `:3440`). The specification's text does not name the method; Part IV renders it from the api. Way back: the probe's drop, question 2's option 1.

content.content:
We say that a value is \emph{an instance of} its runtime
type and of every supertype of its runtime type; immediate subtypes of
\TYP{Any} comprises of tuple types, arrow types, \TYP{()}, \TYP{Object}, and
...
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type
and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType},
...
A tuple type whose element types are all subtypes of the trait \TYP{Index}
is a subtype of \TYP{Index}, the trait of the types that a subscript takes
(\secref{subscripting-ops}).
\TYP{Index} extends \TYP{Any} and not \TYP{Object}
(\secref{trait-decls}),
so such a tuple type is no subtype of \TYP{Object}.

A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type
other than \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Index},
and it excludes \TYP{Index} if and only if one of its element types
excludes \TYP{Index}.
\revision{revival-index}{The Working Draft of February 2011 made no tuple
type a subtype of a trait type, and said that a tuple type excludes any
non-tuple type other than \TYP{Any}. The rule that a tuple of indices is an
\TYP{Index}, and the exclusion that follows from it, are the revival's: they
let an index parameter be bounded by \TYP{Index} while a subscript such as
\EXP{a[i, j]} passes the tuple \EXP{(i, j)} as its one index.}
...
In addition, every trait except \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index}
implicitly extends the trait \TYP{Object}
if it does not do so explicitly.

#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage's comparison: this table (run.sh's) against the last landed one.
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh <last-landed-table|""> <this-table>
#
# Prints one verdict line, then every #kind and #class row whose count moved, with the
# change, and every #crash row that went or came. It is REPORTED and never red: it always
# exits 0, whatever moved, a stale shadow and a run that produced no table included (Pavol,
# answer 11, POSITIONS.md 2026-09-26: a report-only stage, whose job is driving the distance
# down). The verdicts:
#   DISTANCE DOWN|UP|SAME   <last> -> <now>
#   DISTANCE FIRST          no landed table to compare with
#   DISTANCE NO TABLE       this run produced no count, with the table's own reason
#   SETTING CHANGED         the two tables ran different settings: the counts are not like for like
#   SHADOW STALE            a shadow edit no longer matches the tracked sources
# A move of 2 to 4 errors in the components' type errors or in which pair of LEXICO, SQCAP or
# INVERSE declarations an overloading error names is the checker's run-to-run variation
# (switch-over-distance-flat.md section 5), not a change; a crash row whose line numbers
# moved because a rung edited above it prints as one gone and one new.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# compare-sites.py <before.tsv> <after.tsv>: two per-site lists of the distance stage (the landed
# explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv, or errors.py's errors.tsv in a run's scratch folder),
# compared site by site with line numbers masked, and the two export errors entry by entry. Written for
# the array-sites probe (REPORT.md beside it).
def rows(p):
    out = []
    for l in open(p, encoding="utf-8"):
        if l.startswith("#") or not l.strip(): continue
        c = l.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
        out.append(c)
    return out
def mask(s): return re.sub(r"(\.fs[si]):\d+([:.]\d+)?(-\d+(:\d+)?)?", r"\1:L", s)
def key(c):
    kind, loc, msg = c[0], c[5], c[6]
    if kind == "export":
        return (kind, mask(loc), mask(msg.split(":")[0]))
    return (kind, mask(loc), mask(msg))
def entries(msg):
    m = re.search(r"\{(.*)\}\s*$", msg)
    if not m: return []
    body = m.group(1)
    # split on top-level ", " that start an entry: missing declarations end in "at FILE:pos"
    if "Missing declarations" in msg:
        return [mask(e.strip()) for e in re.findall(r"(.*?at FortressLibrary\.fsi:[\d:.-]+)(?:, |$)", body)]
    return [mask(e.strip()) for e in re.findall(r"\((?:ObjectDecl|TraitDecl)[^()]*?(?:\([^()]*\)[^()]*?)*\)", body)]
old, new = rows(sys.argv[1]), rows(sys.argv[2])
ko = collections.Counter(key(c) for c in old); kn = collections.Counter(key(c) for c in new)
print("landed", sum(ko.values()), "now", sum(kn.values()))

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md:110:Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md:132:- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/compiler.md:69:- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/compiler.md:77:- Overloads: the checker reads no bounds of static parameters when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types. So it refuses `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects, and walk loads it (ledger row 786). It accepts `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)`, whose declared domains are equal, and runs the generic one (ledger row 759).
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md:24:- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md:44:  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md:50:  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:13:**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position, so those instances' static arguments are equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair where the equalities leave a static parameter free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`.
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:71:**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only where the call passes a numeral, the checker reads the numeral as `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where the value does not fit.

content.content:
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md:132:- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
20:- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
68:- F-74 **Under walk, an integer numeral takes its type from its value: a `ZZ32` if it fits 32 bits, a `ZZ64` if it fits 64 bits, a `ZZ` above that; it stays so until walk has the checker's static types, since without them a list of numerals and a generic's static argument take their types from the values.** Its run-time type is the library's value object `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum`, below `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:125`, `:128`, `:223`). Walk instantiates a generic at it, so a `Box[\Int\]` is a type apart from `Box[\ZZ32\]` and dispatches past it (row 364). F-74 is why P-76's walk half waits; F-79 is the library half, built. Probe Q (`compile-ladder/plan-n/probe-q/PROBE-Q.md`) measured walk with every integer numeral an `IntLiteral`, the numeral's own type in the library. It ran before climb batch N's second run and before the library half landed. Alone, the switch changed 59 test verdicts. With four devices (a numeral at an `AnyIntegral` parameter read as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ`, a tuple of numerals converted at dispatch, `asif` converting, a varargs list converted at dispatch), the library loaded and both microGPT checks kept their values, but 24 passing interpreter tests failed: 6 by design, 3 of them team tests that assert a `ZZ32`; 9 for want of static types (rows 364, 510); and 9 walk gaps. A size used as a value is a `ZZ32` up to 2^31-1 and a `ZZ64` above (row 486; F-140). Detail: `reviews/numeral-switch-judgement.md` sections 2 and 3.
110:- F-265 **No static parameter of the interpreter's library is bounded by `Object`, so no library declaration meets walk's stop on that bound: under walk, an argument whose type is a tuple, `()` or an arrow, at a parameter whose type is a type variable bounded by `Object`, stops the program with an `InterpreterBug`, not a type error (row 471, open).** The stop needs a bound written `Object`, since walk installs a written bound before it unifies the arguments (row 471). The library's result-only parameters are unbounded, as P-48 decides (F-84). Six functions of `FortressLibrary` write the bound `extends Any`, which admits tuples, `()` and arrows: `cast`, `instanceOf`, `identity`, `shared`, `localize` and `copy` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:33-72`; its api declares the first five so, and holds `copy` in a comment). The specification's examples and the compiler tests write `extends Object` (`SpecData/examples/basic/Fun.Decl.fss:19`, `ProjectFortress/other_compiler_tests/Go1a.fss:15`). Row 471 has no test. Evidence: `git grep -nE '\[\\[^\\]*extends +Object' -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` prints nothing; walk's stop is from the probe that row 471 records, no longer in the tree. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-result-bounds/REPORT.md` section 10.
162:- F-143 **Under walk, a type parameter whose bound mentions itself and that nothing at a call fixes is left open.** Such a bound is an F-bound, as in `mk[\T extends Cmp[\T\]\]()`. The open type, printed `OPEN`, is below every type, and every value matches it. A reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument is first instantiated by its declared type or by its elements' join (F-228). So the open parameter reaches one only where neither fixes it: an empty `SUM` or `PROD` that no declared type directs, which takes `ZZ32`'s identity whatever its body's type (row 716), or a clause form whose declared type or join does not fit the bound (F-228). A call such as `mk()` also leaves it open. Where overloads are compared, a tuple, arrow or generic type that holds the open type admits no more than it would at `BottomType`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` does not take `(1, 2)`, though a lone `one(x: (T,T))` does (row 663, contested). In a probe by the rung's skeptic, the agent that checks a rung's work after its worker, a method declared over `T` in an object whose `T` stayed open was the most specific one, and so was chosen for every argument; no gated test holds this. Gated by `tests/InferUnfixedFBoundedWalk.fss` and `OpenTupleDispatchWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-open-param/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 11; its `SKEPTIC.md` section 3, finding 3 (the probe).
163:- F-144 **The identity-less reductions are typed at their element type: `AssociativeReduction[\R\]` lifts to `Maybe[\R\]`, and its `simpleJoin` and every `lift` take `R`.** A reduction that extends `AssociativeReduction` declares `simpleJoin` at its element type; walk refuses one at `Any` at load. One with static parameters escapes that check and stops at its first join (row 665). A static argument that names the lifted type, as in `generate[\Maybe[\R\]\](...)`, is `Maybe[\R\]`: with `AnyMaybe`, the non-generic trait that `Maybe` extends, the program stops under walk. With the element type unwritten, `BIG MINMAX` and the four tuple forms `BIG MIN_MIN`, `BIG MIN_MAX`, `BIG MAX_MIN` and `BIG MAX_MAX` run under walk. A plain-bounded monoid operator with no static argument is instantiated as F-228 says. So `List`'s `BIG CONCAT` runs, also over a list of list comprehensions. `BIG SQCUP` and `BIG SQCAP` ran in one measurement each, with no gated test, and `PrefixSet`'s `BIG UNION` and `PureList`'s `BIG CONCAT` were not measured. Gated by `tests/UnwrittenBigMinMaxWalk`, `UnwrittenTupleMinMaxWalk`, `UnwrittenBigOperatorsWalk`, `UnwrittenComprehensionElementsWalk` (`List`'s `BIG CONCAT`) and `ReductionSimpleJoinAtAnyWalk` (the refusal at `Any`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-reduction-types/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` section 7 (the operators that ran).

# Rung D (`rung-wrap-operators`): record lines for the gather

Written by the rung worker for the coordinator's fold. *At the gather of climb batch 5 (2026-09-26), where rung D did not land:* the judge's two wording corrections are made ("rung D's edit flips it", "varies with the JVM's flags"; `JUDGE.md` section 5, "Stated more strongly than measured"), nothing here is folded yet, and the provisional numbers 405-407 are not final: the ledger's rows 405-407 are rung S's, so these rows are numbered when D lands. `<D>` stands for the landed commit. Row numbers from 405 are provisional; the gather assigns the final numbers in manifest order (D, S, Z). The rung stopped on one output (section 6 of the report, `XXXInheritedOverload`), which holds the push until Pavol reads it. *At rung D's landing as a follow-up (2026-09-26):* `<D>` is `ab914b6e0`, and the provisional rows 405, 406 and 407 are the ledger's rows 427, 430 and 428. The "Landed semantics" entry and the handover line were folded in `896fae47c`; the notes for rows 403, 348 and 379, the sentence for the entry on fixed-width wrapping and the entry under "The harness and the gate" in the commit after `abe06a743`, the last with the judge's and row 430's wording where this text says more than was measured (the batch record, "Landed as a follow-up").

## FACTS.md

Under "Landed semantics", a new entry after "What relies on fixed-width wrapping under `walk`, and the wrapping operators no running library declares":

- **The specification's wrapping operators under `walk`** (2026-09-26, climb batch 5 rung D, `<D>`; `compile-ladder/rung-wrap-operators/`; rows 348, 403). `DOTPLUS`, `DOTMINUS` (binary and unary) and `DOTTIMES`, the specification's ∔, ∸ and ⨰ (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:172-176`, `:205-209`), are declared abstract on `Integral[\I\]` and with bodies on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, `.fsi`) and `NN32` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`, `.fsi`), each right after its plain operator, bound to wrapping natives of their own, `WrappingAdd`, `WrappingSub`, `WrappingMul` and `WrappingNegate` in `interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java`, `Long.java`, `NN32.java` and `UnsignedLong.java`, whose bodies are the old natives' bodies; on `ZZ` they are bound to the natives `+`, `-` and multiplication use, since on `ZZ` they "do exactly the same thing" (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:369-370`, `:400-401`, `:416`). The library bodies and the six team tests that meant to wrap are respelled with them, fully parenthesised (`Library/RangeInternals.fss`'s six splits, with the strided distance reordered on the checked operators; `Library/Random.fss:235`, `:241`; `Library/ChunkedSparseArray.fss:76`; `Library/IntMap.fss:675-676`; `ProjectFortress/tests/HeapTest.fss`, `intPrim.fss`, `longPrim.fss`, `QuickCheckTest.fss`, `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest.fss`, `UnsignedTest.fss`). Mixed without parentheses with `+`, `BITAND` or each other across the ⨰ boundary, they are refused before evaluation ("Loose operators ... have incomparable precedence"), as `Specification/appendices/operators.tex:27-29` requires; ∔ and ∸ mix left-associatively and ⨰ binds tighter (`:191`, `:213-224`). Gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/WrapOperatorsRungD.fss`. `+`, `-` and multiplication still wrap under `walk` (row 379, batch 6's rung O), and the compiled prelude still spells the pair reversed (row 348's compiled half, at the switch-over). No interpreter test's output changed except by what Q2 = (a) normalises, save `XXXInheritedOverload`'s message order (row 406); the checker count stays 125.

Appended to the entry "What relies on fixed-width wrapping under `walk`, and the wrapping operators no running library declares": *Since rung D (`<D>`), the logging pass over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the demos and the two microGPT checks meets an overflow in none of the eighteen natives except in `XXXFixedWidthOverflowRungB` (row 379's own test, by design), in `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest` through `QQ`'s `opr <`, which must not overflow and answers wrongly when its cross-products wrap (row 407), and in the demo `HeapShakedown` (row 405) (`compile-ladder/rung-wrap-operators/probes/overflow-probe-summary-edit.txt`).*

Under "The harness and the gate", a new entry:

- **The interpreter's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that is not a property of the program** (2026-09-26, climb batch 5 rung D; row 406). On the untouched tree at `6030e4b36`, `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXInheritedOverload.fss` under `walk` with the JVM's default flags names `a(x:Sub1,y:Base)` first in 11 of 16 runs and `a(x:Base,y:Sub2)` first in 5 (`compile-ladder/rung-wrap-operators/probes/order/order-repeat-base.txt`); pinned to one core (`-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1 -XX:+UseSerialGC -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1`, the comparison runner's flags) it is fixed for a given library, and rung D's edit flips it. By reading, the order is that of a `GHashMap` keyed by the methods' signatures, whose hash comes from each `FType`'s global creation counter (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Constructor.java:181-182`, `:325-326`; `values/SingleFcn.java:87-95`; `evaluator/types/FType.java:88-101`). A three-pass output comparison with pinned flags therefore reports this file as stable and changed whenever the library gains declarations; the harness reads only that the `XXX` test fails.

## Ledger

- **Row 403**, appended to its notes, and closed for the sites it names: "Fixed `<D>` (climb batch 5, rung D): the sites it lists are respelled with ∔, ∸ and ⨰, or reordered (the strided distance), and the six team tests with them, every value unchanged (`compile-ladder/rung-wrap-operators/probes/sites/SiteDifferential.txt`, 9,253 checks, 0 differ). The logging pass after the edit meets no overflow in the library sites or the tests this row lists (`compile-ladder/rung-wrap-operators/probes/overflow-probe-summary-edit.txt`). What it still meets is not a wrap the code means: `QQ`'s `opr <` in `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest` (row 407), which the base pass also met (2,352 `Long$Mul` lines without the generator's multiplier, hidden among `LinearCongruential`'s), and row 379's own test. So the count rung O measures is predicted zero except `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest`, which depends on row 407 and on its random data."
- **Row 348**, appended: "Interpreter half fixed `<D>` (climb batch 5, rung D): the one library declares `DOTPLUS`, `DOTMINUS` and `DOTTIMES` with the specification's meaning, bound to wrapping natives (`ProjectFortress/tests/WrapOperatorsRungD.fss`); `walk` no longer says `Operator ? is not defined` for them (`compile-ladder/rung-wrap-operators/probes/failure-preedit.txt` before, `probes/pass-postedit.txt` after). The compiled half, the prelude's reversed spellings in 10 compiled test files, closes at the switch-over; `XXXBoxDotSpellingsRungW` stays its expected failure."
